entries.title: Apollo 11, the first Moon landing
entries.answer: In July 1969, three people traveled to the Moon on Apollo 11. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin rode a small lander called Eagle down to the surface. Michael Collins stayed in their main spacecraft, Columbia, circling overhead. Armstrong and Aldrin took pictures, collected rocks and left instruments behind. They lifted off in the upper part of Eagle and joined Collins again. The three then flew back to Earth and landed in the Pacific Ocean.
facts: Armstrong was the first person to step onto the Moon.

questions.text: How did the astronauts breathe and move outside Eagle?
How do explorers collect samples on Mars without a person to pick them up?
Why does the Moon change shape in our sky?

entries.title: How a phone can find its position using satellites
entries.answer: Navigation satellites broadcast radio signals that say where the satellites are and when the signals left. A receiver compares the signal times. Because the signal travels at a known speed, its travel time helps the receiver estimate its distance from each satellite. Measurements from several satellites let the receiver work out its position, much like finding the crossing point of circles on a map. The satellites do not need a message back from the receiver.
facts: A typical GPS receiver uses at least four satellites to solve for position and correct its own clock.

questions.text: What other jobs can satellites do while circling Earth?
How can numbers tell where a place is east or west?
How does time help us describe distances far beyond Earth?

entries.title: How a spacecraft brought asteroid rocks to Earth
entries.answer: The OSIRIS-REx mission sent a spacecraft to the asteroid Bennu. It studied the surface from nearby before choosing a sampling spot. The spacecraft lowered an arm until its collector briefly touched the ground. A short burst of gas stirred loose material into the collector, and the spacecraft moved away again. It placed the sample in a capsule, which later landed on Earth. Scientists can study each little piece with laboratory instruments.
facts: The sample capsule landed in Utah in 2023.

questions.text: What sorts of materials can make up asteroids?
How do rocks arrive on Earth without being collected by a spacecraft?
How can rocks be carefully sealed on another world first?

entries.title: How a spacesuit keeps an astronaut alive
entries.answer: Outside a spacecraft there is almost no air. A spacesuit for spacewalks is like a tiny spacecraft that moves with a person. It holds air pressure against the body, supplies oxygen and removes used gases. Layers protect the astronaut, and water moving through small tubes in clothing helps carry away heat. A hard helmet lets the astronaut see, while a movable shade cuts down on bright sunlight. Special joints allow the arms and legs to bend.
facts: A backpack can carry the suit’s life-support equipment.

questions.text: Which mission first used suits to walk on the Moon?
Where do crews use suits to work outside an orbiting laboratory?
Why does the body need an air supply?

entries.title: How can a camera above Mars help a rover down below?
entries.answer: The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter looks down from above the planet. Its cameras can make maps sharp enough to show features that a small rover would take a long time to reach. Scientists compare pictures to find good routes and interesting rocks. The spacecraft also uses radio equipment to pick up messages from robots on the surface, then passes the information on to Earth.
facts: A large camera on the spacecraft is called HiRISE.

questions.text: What did Curiosity find in Gale Crater?
How did Phoenix look for water ice at its landing spot?
Why does Perseverance collect and store tubes of rock?

entries.title: How can a laser help a satellite measure ice on Earth?
entries.answer: The ICESat-2 satellite sends tiny flashes of laser light toward Earth. An instrument waits for some of that light to bounce back. A flash returns a little sooner from a higher surface than from a lower one. Timing the trip helps scientists work out the height of ice, land, and water. If they measure the same area again weeks or years later, they can check whether its surface changed.
facts: The satellite can measure how high parts of floating sea ice sit above nearby water.

questions.text: Why does frozen ocean water float at the surface?
How do large bodies of land ice move?
How do other satellites help us look at Earth from above?

entries.title: How could Mercury have ice so close to the Sun?
entries.answer: MESSENGER went into orbit around Mercury and helped confirm there is water ice near the planet’s poles. Some deep holes there have bottoms that sunlight never reaches. Those places stay cold even though sunlit parts of Mercury become extremely hot. The spacecraft looked for signs of hydrogen and compared those readings with maps to tell where the ice was hiding.
facts: MESSENGER became the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury in 2011.

questions.text: How different are Mercury’s days and nights?
Why do spacecraft also map dark craters at the Moon’s poles?
How did a lander confirm ice under soil on Mars?

entries.title: How did Apollo 13 come home after trouble on the way to the Moon?
entries.answer: In April 1970, Apollo 13 was on its way to the Moon when an oxygen tank broke. It damaged part of the spacecraft, so the astronauts gave up the planned landing. They used the small lunar lander as a shelter while they traveled around the Moon and back toward Earth. The crew and teams on the ground worked together to save power and keep the spacecraft safe. All three astronauts returned alive.
facts: The lunar lander that served as a shelter was called Aquarius.

questions.text: How did Apollo’s lunar lander normally reach the Moon?
Which Apollo crew first flew around the Moon?
How did another early capsule return through Earth’s air?

entries.title: How did Chang’e 4 call home from the far side of the Moon?
entries.answer: In January 2019, China’s Chang’e 4 landed on the side of the Moon that faces away from Earth. The Moon blocks a direct radio signal between that landing place and us. A spacecraft named Queqiao flew on a path that gave it a view toward both places. It picked up messages and passed them on. A wheeled robot left the lander to explore the ground.
facts: Chang’e 4 made the first soft landing on the Moon’s far side.

questions.text: Why can’t we normally see the far side from Earth?
Where did India land a rover later?
How can we make maps of places we don’t see from Earth?

entries.title: How did Curiosity find evidence of an old lake on Mars?
entries.answer: Curiosity landed in a wide hollow on Mars called Gale Crater in 2012. It rolled up to rocks, looked at thin layers, and tested bits of material. Some of the rocks were made of very small grains that could settle at the bottom of quiet water. Together with other clues, these rocks helped scientists work out that a lake had once existed in the crater.
facts: A hovering part of the landing system lowered the rover on cords just before it touched the ground.

questions.text: What kinds of rock clues did earlier rovers examine?
Why does a later rover collect tubes of rock?
What did another spacecraft find below the Martian ground?

entries.title: How did Gaia help build a three-dimensional map of the Milky Way?
entries.answer: The European Space Agency’s Gaia spacecraft measured where stars appeared in the sky. It took measurements again and again as it moved along with Earth around the Sun. Some nearby stars appeared to shift very slightly against more distant ones when viewed from different places. That shift helped scientists find their distances. The measurements also helped show how stars move through our galaxy.
facts: Gaia’s maps cover more than a billion stars.

questions.text: Where does our solar system sit in the Milky Way?
How do we describe huge distances between stars?
How can measuring starlight reveal a planet instead?

entries.title: How did Hayabusa2 bring bits of an asteroid back to Earth?
entries.answer: Japan sent the Hayabusa2 spacecraft to visit Ryugu, a small asteroid whose surface is covered with rocks. The spacecraft came down close enough to take some of the material from it. It kept the samples in a sealed container for the flight back. In 2020 a small capsule carrying the samples landed in Australia. Researchers could use laboratory equipment on Earth to look closely at material from another world.
facts: The main spacecraft released the capsule while passing Earth and continued flying through space.

questions.text: Which other mission brought back pieces of an asteroid?
How did Dawn use instruments without bringing rocks home?
How did another spacecraft send a small lander to a comet?

entries.title: How did Kepler notice planets it could not photograph?
entries.answer: NASA’s Kepler space telescope watched many stars and measured how bright they looked. If a planet crossed in front of a star as seen from the telescope, it could block a little light. A tiny dip that happened again and again gave scientists a clue that a planet might be there. The mission found many planets outside our solar system, including some smaller than Neptune.
facts: The original Kepler survey watched one main patch of sky for years.

questions.text: What is a planet beyond our solar system?
Why did a later telescope study bright stars across much more of the sky?
How can measuring star positions answer a different question?

entries.title: How did Magellan map land it could not see through the clouds?
entries.answer: NASA’s Magellan orbited Venus in the 1990s. Thick clouds hide the ground from cameras that see ordinary light. Magellan sent radio waves toward the surface instead. It listened for the waves that bounced back and used them to build up pictures of the ground. These radar pictures showed mountains, old impact holes, and shapes made by lava across much of the planet.
facts: Scientists can use radar to make an image without sunlight.

questions.text: What did an earlier spacecraft measure about Venus’s temperature?
What conditions make it hard to see the ground on Venus?
How can a camera map details on a less cloudy planet?

entries.title: How did Mariner 2 learn that Venus is very hot?
entries.answer: Mariner 2 flew past Venus in 1962. Thick clouds hide the planet’s ground in ordinary photographs, but the spacecraft could measure invisible waves coming from Venus. The readings supported the idea that the surface below those clouds is very hot. Mariner 2 did not land or circle the planet. Its instruments took measurements as the spacecraft passed, then it continued traveling around the Sun.
facts: Mariner 2 made the first successful scientific flyby of another planet.

questions.text: Why is the ground on Venus hotter than Earth’s?
How did a later mission map the surface through its clouds?
What did a flyby show at a much colder world?

entries.title: How did Mars Pathfinder let a little rover roll on Mars?
entries.answer: Mars Pathfinder reached Mars in July 1997. It came down on the ground inside cushions filled with gas, then opened up to let a small rover named Sojourner out. The rover could roll up to nearby rocks, look at them closely, and help scientists study what they were made of. Instead of carrying a large radio for a direct link to Earth, Sojourner sent its information to the lander nearby.
facts: Sojourner rolled on six wheels.

questions.text: What did earlier landers learn without driving around?
What did two larger rovers discover about water?
How did a heavy rover land by a different method?

entries.title: How did people make the Mir space station bigger in orbit?
entries.answer: Mir started with one section sent to orbit in 1986. Later flights brought other rooms and work areas to join to it. Putting the parts together in space meant the whole station did not need to fit inside one rocket. Crews could live on Mir while working on experiments. In the 1990s, U.S. space shuttles came to the station to bring people and supplies.
facts: Mir’s first section came from the Soviet Union.

questions.text: What did crews do on the early U.S. station?
How did later crews use the International Space Station?
How did a space shuttle return to Earth?

entries.title: How did Spitzer see through some clouds of space dust?
entries.answer: Spitzer was a NASA space telescope that collected infrared light, which human eyes cannot see. Some infrared light gets through dust that can hide stars from an ordinary telescope. That let Spitzer pick out young stars in dusty clouds. It also measured infrared light from distant planets and galaxies. Different kinds of light give scientists different clues, so they often compare pictures taken by several telescopes.
facts: Spitzer began its mission in 2003.

questions.text: What can a telescope learn from X-rays?
Why does Webb also look in infrared light?
What other telescope studied very cool gas and dust?

entries.title: How did two twin rovers find signs that Mars had once been wet?
entries.answer: Spirit and Opportunity reached opposite parts of Mars in 2004. They studied features in rocks and soil that could tell a story about water long ago. Opportunity saw tiny round pieces rich in a mineral whose shape and location were clues to how the rock had formed. The two rovers were designed for a few months of work, and both kept sending back results for much longer.
facts: When the little round pieces appeared in photographs, scientists nicknamed them blueberries.

questions.text: Which smaller robot proved a rover could drive on Mars?
How did another rover read the story of a whole lake?
How can photos from above help scientists plan a rover’s trip?

entries.title: How Ingenuity flew in the thin air of Mars
entries.answer: The small helicopter Ingenuity rode to Mars under the Perseverance rover. The air on Mars is much thinner than on Earth, so there are fewer gas molecules for rotor blades to push against. Ingenuity used large, light blades that spun very quickly for its size. Its first flights showed that a powered craft could take off, steer and land on another planet. It later flew ahead to photograph ground that might matter to the rover crew.
facts: Ingenuity completed 72 flights on Mars.

questions.text: How does a helicopter on Earth push itself upward?
Which rover delivered the helicopter and used some of its views?
Why does a moving blade need air to produce lift?

entries.title: How many times did John Glenn circle Earth in Friendship 7?
entries.answer: In 1962, John Glenn rode a small spacecraft named Friendship 7 around Earth three times. He was the first American to go into orbit. Other American astronauts had already reached space, but their short trips came back before making a full circle. Glenn stayed in space for just under five hours. A thick shield helped protect his capsule from heat as it rushed back through Earth’s air.
facts: The capsule landed in the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.text: Who had already orbited Earth before Glenn’s flight?
Why do people seem to float when they are in orbit?
When did crewed flights go farther and circle the Moon?

entries.title: How spacecraft borrow speed from planets
entries.answer: Passing near a moving planet can change the path of a spacecraft. The planet’s gravity bends the spacecraft’s path as it flies past. Seen from the Sun, the spacecraft may leave faster or slower than it arrived, depending on which way it went past the planet. The planet’s motion changes by a tiny amount in return, too small to notice. Mission planners use these carefully chosen flybys to reach destinations that would otherwise need more fuel.
facts: A gravity assist can change direction as well as speed.

questions.text: Which pair of explorers used planet flybys to cross the outer solar system?
Which massive planet has helped send many spacecraft farther outward?
How is flying past a world different from circling it repeatedly?

entries.title: How weather satellites watch moving storms
entries.answer: Weather satellites photograph Earth and measure kinds of light our eyes cannot see. A satellite high above the equator can go around once each day in the same direction as Earth turns. It appears to stay over one region, taking many pictures of a storm as it moves. Other satellites circle closer to Earth and pass near the poles. As Earth turns beneath them, those satellites can see different strips of the planet.
facts: Infrared measurements help show clouds and temperature patterns even at night.

questions.text: What storm changes are easier to spot with repeated pictures?
How can satellites have useful jobs besides forecasting weather?
What makes the clouds seen in satellite images?

entries.title: Life aboard the International Space Station
entries.answer: The International Space Station is a science laboratory moving around Earth. Rockets carried its rooms and large pieces up one at a time. Crews watch Earth below them and do experiments with plants, liquids and materials. The station gets electricity from sunlight falling on large solar panels. Inside, almost everything has to be held in place because it can float. Crew members exercise regularly because their muscles and bones do less work in orbit.
facts: The first pieces of the station were launched and joined in 1998.

questions.text: Why do people and their tools float inside the station?
What do astronauts wear when repairs take them outside?
How can sunlight supply electricity aboard a spacecraft?

entries.title: Perseverance, a robot geologist on Mars
entries.answer: Perseverance is a car-sized robot that landed in Jezero Crater in 2021. That place has a fan of rock left where a river once carried material into a lake. The rover studies those rocks for clues about the old lake and whether there could have been tiny living things long ago. Cameras help it choose objects to study. A drill can take a narrow cylinder of rock, which the rover seals in a metal tube.
facts: Collecting a promising rock sample is different from proving that life was ever there.

questions.text: What made Mars different when liquid water flowed across parts of it?
What clues can layers of rock hold?
How did people collect rock samples before a Mars rover tried it?

entries.title: The Hubble Space Telescope
entries.answer: Hubble carries a polished mirror and cameras as it circles Earth. The mirror gathers light and brings it together so instruments can record very faint objects. Being in space means it looks through much less air than telescopes on the ground. That removes much of the blurring and lets its instruments detect some kinds of light that air blocks. Astronauts visited Hubble to fix parts and install better cameras while it was still in orbit.
facts: Hubble can observe visible light as well as some ultraviolet and infrared light.

questions.text: Why does Webb use a very large sunshield?
What are the huge star systems that telescopes photograph?
How can light be brought to a focus by curved glass?

entries.title: The James Webb Space Telescope
entries.answer: Webb is a space telescope made to study infrared light. That light is invisible to our eyes, but Webb can record it. Infrared light helps it look through some clouds of dust where stars are forming. Its main mirror is made from 18 pieces that unfolded after launch. A great shield with five layers keeps much of the warmth from the Sun, Earth and Moon away from the instruments, so the telescope can detect faint signals.
facts: The mirror has a thin layer of gold that reflects infrared light well.

questions.text: Why was Hubble also placed above Earth’s air?
What can telescopes learn about worlds around other stars?
How can light carry warmth through empty space?

entries.title: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2
entries.answer: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 left Earth in 1977 to study the outer planets. The spacecraft flew close enough to take detailed pictures without landing. Together they visited Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, although only Voyager 2 went to the last two. A carefully planned path let a close pass by one planet change a spacecraft’s speed and direction. Each carries a Golden Record with sounds, music and pictures from Earth.
facts: Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft to have flown close to Uranus and Neptune as of 2026.

questions.text: What strange features did Voyager 2 see on Neptune’s largest moon?
What patterns did it photograph near Uranus?
How can a passing planet change a spacecraft’s course?

entries.title: What artificial satellites do
entries.answer: An artificial satellite is an object people built and put into orbit. Some satellites collect pictures showing where clouds are growing, where wildfires have spread or how much ice covers the ground. Others pass radio messages between distant places. A satellite can watch an area repeatedly, making changes easier to spot. It needs the right sideways speed to stay in orbit. It usually gets power from sunlight and sends its measurements back to ground stations.
facts: The Moon is a natural satellite because it orbits Earth and people did not build it.

questions.text: How does falling sideways fast enough make an orbit?
How do spacecraft make electricity from sunlight?
What can astronauts study from a laboratory in orbit?

entries.title: What can a spacecraft map from above the Moon?
entries.answer: NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter flies around the Moon. It makes maps and pictures that reveal details such as rough ground, craters, and areas near the poles that stay in shadow. Scientists use the shape and brightness of those places to understand how they formed and to identify interesting sites for future visits. A map can help a crew look for a smooth spot to land before it leaves Earth.
facts: The mission began in 2009.

questions.text: How did astronauts explore after reaching the surface?
How did a spacecraft land where Earth cannot see it directly?
How did the large dark plains on the Moon form?

entries.title: What could Cassini learn by going around Saturn for years?
entries.answer: The Cassini spacecraft began orbiting Saturn in 2004. Instead of seeing the planet and its rings on a single pass, it could watch as things changed and visit different moons. Cassini observed jets of material coming from the icy moon Enceladus. It also brought a smaller spacecraft named Huygens to land on Titan. At the end of its mission, Cassini flew into Saturn’s atmosphere.
facts: Saturn’s rings are made mostly of pieces of ice.

questions.text: What did Huygens see below Titan’s haze?
What might be below the icy surface of Enceladus?
What are Saturn’s rings made of?

entries.title: What did Galileo learn by circling Jupiter?
entries.answer: NASA’s Galileo spacecraft entered orbit around Jupiter in 1995. It could pass many times through the region around the planet and study several moons up close. Measurements near Europa pointed to a salty ocean hidden below the ice. A smaller part of the mission plunged into Jupiter’s clouds and sent back measurements as it went deeper. The main spacecraft kept flying around Jupiter after the probe stopped.
facts: Galileo was the first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter.

questions.text: Why do scientists think Europa has hidden water?
What did Juno find near Jupiter’s poles?
Which spacecraft first flew past Jupiter?

entries.title: What did Huygens find under Titan’s orange haze?
entries.answer: Huygens was a small European spacecraft carried to Saturn by Cassini. In 2005 it drifted down to Titan by parachute as cameras and instruments studied the thick air. Below the haze, it saw hills cut by dark channels. The lander touched down on a surface scattered with rounded pieces that may be water ice. Huygens sent its measurements to Cassini for the trip back to Earth by radio.
facts: Titan is Saturn’s largest moon.

questions.text: How did Cassini carry Huygens to Saturn?
How can liquids shape Titan’s surface when it is too cold for liquid water?
How did a different small spacecraft land on Mars?

entries.title: What did India send to the Moon on Chandrayaan-3?
entries.answer: India’s Chandrayaan-3 mission put a lander named Vikram on the Moon in 2023. A small rover named Pragyan rolled down a ramp and checked the soil and rocks near the landing spot. The spacecraft touched down far south of the Moon’s middle, in a highland area near its south pole. The rover’s instruments could look for elements in the soil while staying close to the lander.
facts: Chandrayaan-3 was India’s first successful soft landing on the Moon.

questions.text: How can an orbiter help a team map its landing area?
Which other country first landed on the Moon’s far side?
How did people use a rover on the Moon?

entries.title: What did InSight learn by listening to the ground on Mars?
entries.answer: InSight landed on Mars and placed a sensitive instrument on the ground. A seismometer can notice tiny shakes that people might not feel. The shakes from marsquakes traveled through the planet at different speeds. Researchers used their arrival times to learn about layers deep under the surface, including the central core. The spacecraft could discover these clues while staying in one place and waiting for a shake.
facts: Researchers also used vibrations from space rocks that struck Mars.

questions.text: What makes the ground shake on Earth?
How can looking at rocks answer a different question about Mars?
How can a spacecraft find changes in the surface while staying in orbit?

entries.title: What did New Horizons find when it flew past Pluto?
entries.answer: In July 2015, NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft made the first close visit to Pluto. It found mountains and a broad bright region shaped like part of a heart. The bright plain there contains frozen nitrogen. New Horizons moved past Pluto instead of stopping in orbit. Years later, it passed Arrokoth, a smaller object in the Kuiper Belt that looks like two rounded pieces joined together.
facts: Signals from the Pluto encounter took hours to travel back to Earth.

questions.text: Why is Pluto called a dwarf planet?
What other small worlds travel beyond Neptune?
What could a single fast pass reveal at Jupiter?

entries.title: What did Phoenix find when it dug into Martian dirt?
entries.answer: Phoenix stayed in one spot near the northern part of Mars. In 2008 it used a moving arm to dig into the soil, scooping up bits for its instruments. Nearby, scientists saw bright pieces that disappeared after being exposed to the air. The pieces were another clue that water ice lay just below the surface. Its measurements helped confirm the ice. Phoenix stayed put instead of driving away like a rover.
facts: Unlike a rover, Phoenix did not drive away from its landing place.

questions.text: What is Mars like near its poles?
How did a different lander study the inside of Mars?
How can a spacecraft study Mars from above the ground?

entries.title: What did the Apollo 8 crew see when they flew around the Moon?
entries.answer: In December 1968, NASA sent three astronauts on a trip around the Moon. They were the first people to see the Moon up close from orbit. Their spacecraft passed over the far side, the side we usually cannot see from Earth. During the trip, the astronauts saw Earth come into view above the gray Moon. A photo taken by crew member Bill Anders became known as Earthrise.
facts: Apollo 8 circled the Moon ten times without landing.

questions.text: Why does the same side of the Moon usually face Earth?
Which mission first put people on the Moon’s surface?
How did astronauts later drive across the Moon?

entries.title: What did the Viking landers do on Mars?
entries.answer: In 1976, two Viking missions brought U.S. spacecraft to the surface of Mars. Each mission included a spacecraft that stayed in orbit and another that landed. The landers took pictures, checked the weather, and studied soil. Some experiments looked for signs of life, but their results did not show clear proof that anything was alive there. Each lander remained at its landing spot and could send pictures back from the same place over time.
facts: Later Mars rovers could move between different spots on the surface.

questions.text: Which later lander carried a small rover that could move?
What is the surface of Mars like?
How did a later rover find signs of an ancient lake?

entries.title: What happened to some of the air Mars once had?
entries.answer: NASA’s MAVEN spacecraft flew around Mars and studied the thin air high above the ground. It measured how particles escape into space. Light from the Sun and streams of particles from it can help knock parts of the outer air away. Those measurements gave scientists clues about how Mars lost much of its atmosphere over a very long time. The thinner air affects what happens to liquid water at the surface.
facts: MAVEN began circling Mars in 2014.

questions.text: What is the air and weather like on Mars today?
What does the Sun send out besides light?
What evidence shows that long ago Mars had liquid water?

entries.title: What kinds of cold places did Herschel study in space?
entries.answer: The Herschel observatory studied long waves of infrared light from cold gas and dust, neither of which has to shine brightly to give off such light. It could look at clouds where new stars were beginning to form before they were easy to see in ordinary photographs. It could also find signs of molecules in space. Herschel’s large mirror helped gather weak light from distant places.
facts: Herschel was a European Space Agency observatory with a mirror about 3.5 meters wide.

questions.text: Which other observatory used infrared to study hidden stars?
What is a cloud of gas and dust in space?
How did a separate European mission measure star positions?

entries.title: What kinds of things can Chandra see with X-rays?
entries.answer: The Chandra X-ray Observatory is a telescope in space. It looks for X-rays that some extremely hot places give off. These rays come from regions such as gas around a black hole or material heated by a star’s explosion. Earth’s air blocks most X-rays from space, so Chandra works above it. Observations like these can show parts of the sky that ordinary cameras would miss.
facts: A shuttle brought Chandra to space in 1999.

questions.text: Why can material near a black hole give off light?
What happens when a star explodes?
What can a space telescope see in a different kind of invisible light?

entries.title: What path did Pioneer 10 take to reach Jupiter?
entries.answer: Pioneer 10 left Earth in 1972 and became the first spacecraft to pass through the main asteroid belt. It then flew by Jupiter and sent back close measurements of the great planet and its surroundings. Before that trip, scientists knew about Jupiter’s colors from pictures made much closer to home. Pioneer 10 could measure conditions near the planet itself, and helped NASA plan later trips far from Earth.
facts: A later spacecraft named Pioneer 11 passed Jupiter on its way to Saturn.

questions.text: Where is the main asteroid belt?
How did going into orbit let Galileo study more than one pass?
Which two spacecraft followed on more distant journeys?

entries.title: What surprising clue did Explorer 1 find above Earth?
entries.answer: Explorer 1 was the first U.S. satellite, launched in January 1958. One instrument counted energetic particles. The counts sometimes dropped to zero in places where scientists had expected to find some particles. The researchers worked out that the instrument could be getting more hits than it could count, rather than no hits at all. Later measurements helped confirm a radiation belt around Earth, where our planet’s magnetic field holds many energetic particles.
facts: Explorer 1 was a long narrow spacecraft with instruments built into its body.

questions.text: How did Sputnik let people know it was flying overhead?
What kinds of particles come from the Sun?
Who was the first human to orbit Earth?

entries.title: What was it like to live and work in Skylab?
entries.answer: Skylab was the first U.S. space station. Astronauts visited it in 1973 and 1974 to study the Sun, try experiments, and see what happens to people who live in orbit for weeks. Part of the station was hurt during launch, leaving it too warm. The first crew put up a shade and made other repairs. That made the station a place they could work and sleep in.
facts: The third Skylab crew lived in space for about 84 days.

questions.text: How was Mir built from pieces joined in orbit?
What do astronauts do on the International Space Station?
Why did things float inside Skylab?

entries.title: Who rode Vostok 1 around Earth?
entries.answer: In April 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human to travel into space. He rode in a round cabin on a Soviet spacecraft called Vostok 1. It went around Earth once before coming back down. Only a few years earlier, Sputnik had gone into orbit with no one aboard. Gagarin’s journey showed that a person could travel all the way around our planet in space and return.
facts: A Russian space traveler is often called a cosmonaut.

questions.text: What object went around Earth before people did?
Who was the first American to orbit Earth?
Who first flew around the Moon?

entries.title: Why a spacecraft flew through the Sun’s outer atmosphere
entries.answer: The Parker Solar Probe was built to study the Sun from closer than any earlier spacecraft. Its wide heat shield stays pointed toward the Sun, keeping much of the direct radiation off the instruments behind it. Sensors measure particles and magnetic fields in the Sun’s outer atmosphere. This helps scientists investigate how material flowing away becomes the solar wind. The spacecraft visits the hot region and then continues along its curved orbit.
facts: The probe first passed through the Sun’s outer atmosphere, called the corona, in 2021.

questions.text: What is the moving material the spacecraft studies?
What happens when magnetic fields affect temperatures on the visible Sun?
Why is a shield helpful even between a spacecraft and a distant hot object?

entries.title: Why did Apollo 15 take a car to the Moon?
entries.answer: Apollo 15 landed on the Moon in 1971. The crew took a small electric vehicle called a lunar rover, so they could visit spots far beyond their landing place. They drove near mountains and a deep channel, took photographs, and collected rocks. The vehicle folded up for the trip to the Moon. Unfolding it gave the astronauts a way to carry tools and samples without taking every step on foot.
facts: Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather. Without much air on the Moon to slow the feather, both landed together.

questions.text: How did the first team reach the lunar surface?
How can a spacecraft map the Moon without landing?
How did a small robot get around on Mars?

entries.title: Why did Dawn orbit two different worlds in the asteroid belt?
entries.answer: Dawn traveled to Vesta and Ceres, two large worlds in the asteroid belt. Vesta is mostly rocky. Ceres has more water and shows a very different surface. Dawn carried instruments that could map the shapes and test what different parts of each world were made of. Visiting both helped scientists compare what happened to two objects that formed in the same broad neighborhood of the solar system.
facts: Dawn went into orbit at Vesta in 2011 and at Ceres in 2015.

entries.title: Why did Ed White step outside Gemini 4?
entries.answer: In 1965, astronaut Ed White opened a hatch and moved outside the Gemini 4 spacecraft. He wore a suit that supplied air and protected him from the space around him. A line kept him joined to the spacecraft while he floated beside it. White tested how it felt to move out there. Knowing how to work outside a spacecraft would help later crews build and fix things in orbit.
facts: White’s trip outside was the first spacewalk by an American astronaut.

entries.title: Why did Juno fly over Jupiter’s poles?
entries.answer: Juno circles Jupiter on a path that passes over the north and south poles. This gave its cameras a view of places that are difficult to see from Earth. The spacecraft showed storms gathered around both poles. Other instruments studied the planet’s magnetic field and measured microwaves to study the atmosphere beneath the bright cloud tops. Jupiter has no solid ground for a rover to drive across.
facts: Many of Jupiter’s big storms are part of patterns scientists can track from orbit.

entries.title: Why did people listen for the beeps of Sputnik 1?
entries.answer: In October 1957, the Soviet Union sent a small metal ball into orbit around Earth. It was called Sputnik 1 and was the first artificial satellite. Its thin antennas sent a repeating radio signal. People on the ground could use radio equipment to hear it as a stream of beeps. A device made on Earth was now going around our planet again and again, much as the Moon does.
facts: Sputnik 1 was about as wide as a large beach ball.

entries.title: Why did Rosetta travel beside a comet around the Sun?
entries.answer: Rosetta was a European spacecraft that caught up with a comet named 67P. It stayed near the comet for many months. As their path carried them closer to the Sun, Rosetta could watch gas such as water vapor and tiny bits of dust escape from the warming surface. It also sent a little lander called Philae down to take measurements. Studying a comet for a long time can show changes that a single flyby would miss.
facts: Rosetta reached the comet in 2014 after traveling for about ten years.

entries.title: Why did the space shuttle have wings?
entries.answer: NASA’s space shuttle rose into the sky with rocket power and worked in orbit as a spacecraft. At the end of a trip, the winged part came back through the air and glided onto a runway. It did not use jet engines to land. NASA could prepare that part to fly again. The shuttle carried satellites and helped build the International Space Station by bringing up large pieces.
facts: The reusable winged part was called the orbiter.

entries.title: Why did Voyager take a record of sounds from Earth?
entries.answer: Each Voyager spacecraft carries a disc with sounds and pictures chosen to show something about Earth. It includes noises from nature, greetings in many languages, and different kinds of music. A person on Earth could play a record with the right equipment and hear the sounds. Nobody knows if anyone far away will find either disc. The record was also a way for people on Earth to think about what they would want to share.
facts: The two discs are made of copper with a coating of gold.

entries.title: Why do astronauts float in orbit?
entries.answer: Earth’s gravity pulls on an orbiting astronaut and the spacecraft around them. Both are falling toward Earth, but both are traveling sideways so fast that Earth’s curved surface keeps dropping away beneath them. Because the astronaut and the cabin are falling together, the floor hardly pushes on their feet. A loose pencil stays nearby for the same reason. The feeling can be like a short drop on a ride, except it lasts while the craft keeps orbiting.
facts: Gravity keeps the space station in orbit, even while people inside feel weightless.

entries.title: Why does TESS search for planets around bright stars?
entries.answer: The TESS telescope looks at a large part of the sky in sections. It measures the light of stars, looking for small dips when possible planets cross their faces. The mission helps find planets around nearby bright stars. A planet is usually easier for other telescopes to study when its star is bright enough to give them a stronger signal. Follow-up observations help scientists check which tiny dips really came from planets.
facts: TESS stands for Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite.
